description: Team Ad Lunam from the Space City! We're a crew of computer, aerospace, electrical engineers and astronomy enthusiasts ready to launch our ideas at the NASA hackathon.
summary:
Moonslip is a web app for the question a lunar mission team faces after a schedule change: if the landing slips, what do we lose, and why? Choose a landing site, a date, the days on the surface and a slip, and it shows the hours with the Sun above the local terrain skyline (power), the hours with Earth in view (direct-to-Earth radio) and the hours with both. It then explains each change in plain words: the lunar day/night cycle, Earth's libration, or the terrain that blocks the view, with its compass direction and distance. It also finds the next equally good landing date and ranks the alternatives.

Existing tools give accurate Sun and Earth positions, but one site and one query at a time, without terrain or explanation. Moonslip compares 21 sourced sites and any custom coordinate over 2023 to 2030, entirely in the browser.

Small slips have large effects. Re-enacting Intuitive Machines' IM-1 with a 7-day stay, a 10-day slip cuts the hours with Sun and Earth in view from 155.5 to 82.0, and the next equally good date is 30 days after the plan. Every Sun and Earth position is checked against NASA JPL Horizons.
details:
Quick links: 28-second demo video · 7 slides (Google Slides) · the live site · source code (MIT)

The problem

A lunar lander needs sunlight for power and a line of sight to Earth for direct radio contact. Near the poles the Sun skims the horizon, so a hill a few degrees tall can hide it for days, and Earth rises and sets as the Moon rocks on its orbit (libration). When a launch slips, the lighting and communication picture at the landing site changes, sometimes by a lot. NASA's Artemis site-selection team says more than one candidate landing region must be kept to allow flexibility in launch timing, and that regions with greater Earth visibility are preferred (George et al., LPSC 2026).

The tools for this exist but are hard to use for this question: NASA JPL Horizons answers one site and one time range per query, as a text table, with no terrain. Planners want the consequence of a slip, and the reason for it, in seconds.

What Moonslip does

Figure 1. How a user goes from a question to a decision.

  • Verdict. A one-line answer at the top ("If IM-1 Odysseus lands 10 days late, Sun + Earth time falls from 155.5 h to 82.0 h. Next date as good: +30 d."), then four numbers: hours before and after the slip, the change with its terrain-error range, the main reason, and the next equally good date.
  • Cause lines. Every gain or loss is split into an orbital part and one part per blocking terrain feature, each with its azimuth and distance.
  • Your options, ranked. The planned date, the slipped date, the next date that is as good as the plan, and nearby terrain-modelled sites, as bars sorted by hours with Sun and Earth in view. Each row opens to show its cause lines.
  • Best dates to land. Every landing date for the next 13 months, with the three best dates marked; clicking a date tries it.
  • All terrain sites by landing date. A site-by-date map of hours with Sun and Earth in view for the six sites with a terrain skyline.
  • Earth above the skyline for 30 days, an hour-by-hour timeline, and a 360° view from the site with the terrain skyline, the Sun and Earth paths and the blocking terrain labelled.
  • Compare sites. One small Sun / Earth / both strip per site for the same date, sorted by hours, plus a sortable table.
  • 3D mission simulator. The lander at its site with the Sun and Earth in the sky, playable through the stay, with power and communication readouts.
  • For educators and the public: an Explain mode with plain-language notes and a five-step guided tour. For reviews: a printable brief, and a link that stores the whole scenario.
  • Custom site: any latitude and longitude on the Moon, with a smooth-sphere horizon that is labelled as such.

Worked example: Intuitive Machines IM-1 (Houston)

IM-1's January 2024 launch window was lost to changes in the launch manifest, and the mission landed in February, because its site near Malapert A is only well lit for part of each month. Lighting did not cause the slip; it turned a slip of days into a slip of a month. Moonslip shows that in one screen.

Figure 2. Hours with Sun and Earth in view for a 7-day stay at the IM-1 site, for every landing time from 5 January to 5 March 2024, computed from the project's data. Whiskers show the range when the terrain is raised or lowered by its published height error. Earth stays in view the whole time at this site, so the curve equals the sunlit hours. The 19 January date is an illustrative baseline inside the original window.

  • Planned, 19 Jan 2024 23:24 UTC (illustrative): 155.5 h with Sun and Earth in view (148.8 to 157.0 h across the terrain error).
  • Landing 10 days late, 29 Jan: 82.0 h (81.7 to 82.3 h). Main reason given by the app: lunar night, orbit not terrain (−69.0 h).
  • Next date as good, 18 Feb (+30 days): 163.0 h (156.2 to 164.5 h).

The actual landing on 22 February 2024 at 23:24 UTC sits on the next plateau: a 7-day stay from that time gets the full 168 hours.

How it works

Figure 3. Data flow. The Python pipeline runs once and writes small static files; everything the visitor sees is computed in the browser from those files.

  • Sun and Earth positions. NASA NAIF SPICE kernels (DE440 planetary ephemeris and the DE440 lunar orientation) give the Sun and Earth vectors in the Moon's mean-Earth frame, hourly from 1 January 2023 to 31 December 2030: 70,128 rows in a 1.96 MB file. The browser interpolates between hours and computes Earth's direction from the landing site, not from the Moon's centre. That difference reaches 0.28° and moves Earthrise by hours near the poles.
  • Terrain skylines. For six sites (IM-1, IM-2, Chandrayaan-3, Connecting Ridge and two Shackleton rim points) the pipeline traces 720 directions out to 220 km over NASA LOLA elevation models, allowing for the Moon's curvature, from 2 m above the ground. Grids: 40 m at IM-1, IM-2 and the Shackleton rim points, a 5 m site model at Connecting Ridge, 240 m at Chandrayaan-3. For each direction it keeps the terrain cell that sets the skyline, which is what lets the app say where a blocker is. The other 15 sites use a smooth-sphere horizon, and the app labels them that way.
  • Visibility. A body counts as in view when any part of its disc clears the skyline (a setting switches to half the disc). Each stay is sampled every 10 minutes.
  • Uncertainty. Each skyline is recomputed with the terrain raised and lowered by NASA's published per-pixel height error, and the results carry that range. The error from grid spacing is not included.
  • No server. A static site (TypeScript, Vite, three.js for the simulator) deployed on GitHub Pages; the pipeline is Python (spiceypy, rasterio, pyproj, NumPy, SciPy). Code: github.com/aryasira/nasa (MIT licence).

How a cause line is computed

Figure 4. For each body, the change in hours in view is split into three parts that add up exactly. Example from IM-1 with a 10-day slip: "Sun lost 69.0 h: lunar day/night cycle (not terrain)".

The orbital part is the change in hours above a flat, terrain-free horizon. Each terrain part is the change in hours hidden by one blocker; named blockers get their IAU name from the USGS Gazetteer, others are labelled "unnamed terrain". The site-height part counts hours seen below a flat horizon because the site stands above its surroundings. A test checks that the parts sum to the total change for each body.

How we know it is right

Figure 5. Largest difference from NASA JPL Horizons at each site, on a logarithmic scale, recomputed from the project's data.

  • JPL Horizons. 160 Sun and Earth positions at seven landing sites located by NASA's LRO cameras all agree with NASA JPL Horizons within 0.01°. The largest gap is 0.0009°, about 1/550 of the Sun's width. The live site repeats this check in the visitor's browser.
  • A published study. Over 2023 to 2030 our model has the Sun in view at Connecting Ridge 91.25% of the time (88.18% to 93.09% across the terrain error). Gläser et al. (2014) found 92.27% at 2 m over 19 years on a 20 m terrain model. The spans and terrain models differ, so this is a plausibility check; the published value lies inside our range.
  • Two independent engines. The browser engine is tested against a separate Python reference implementation on shared test vectors, and against the Horizons positions.

Who it is for

  • Mission planners and site-selection teams: the cost of a slip, the reason, the next good date and a brief for a review.
  • Educators, students and the public: Explain mode, the guided tour and the simulator show why the poles are hard and why small date changes matter.

What is illustrative, and what is not modelled

  • "In view" means line of sight only. Lander tilt, solar-panel pointing, thermal limits, radio link budgets and relay satellites are not modelled. Power figures are geometry, not a power model.
  • 15 of the 21 sites use a smooth-sphere horizon. Near the poles, real terrain can change those results a lot; the app says so for each such site.
  • Relief smaller than the terrain grid (5 m to 240 m depending on the site) is not resolved, and the uncertainty range does not include it.
  • In the simulator, the skyline comes from the terrain data; ground detail, rocks, the Earth pattern and the stars are illustrative.
  • The 19 January 2024 IM-1 baseline is an illustrative date inside the original window.

What is new, and next steps

Slip sliders, terrain horizons and Horizons checks exist in other tools and other teams' projects. What we have not seen elsewhere is a tool that explains each lost or gained window in words, splits orbit from terrain exactly, and shows the knock-on wait for the next equally good date.

Next: terrain skylines for more sites, a mast-height setting, Chang'e 7's 2026 postponement as a second worked example, and an estimate of the hours a lander must survive after sunset.

Use of AI

We used AI heavily and say so inside the project as well: source files drafted with AI carry an "AI-assisted" header, every data file carries meta.ai_generated: true, and the README and the site footer state it.

  • Research (Anthropic Claude): AI-assisted research to read the challenge, survey NASA data sources, check facts (mission coordinates, kernels, terrain products, published benchmarks) and review other teams' public projects and past winners. Those notes proposed the slip-impact and cause-line direction, which the team chose to build.
  • Code (Claude Code): most of the pipeline, engine, interface and tests were drafted by AI in three separate sessions (data and science; engine and app; integration, testing and writing), each allowed to change only its own files, with fixed data formats between them. A team member reviewed and merged every change through pull requests on GitHub and ran the data pipeline on their own computer. A separate AI session reviewed the work; its findings are in REVIEW.md in the repository.
  • Text: AI drafted the documentation and this project description.
  • Images: no AI image generator was used. The charts and the simulator are drawn by the app's code, and the diagrams here were drawn with Python from the project's data. No NASA logos or insignia appear anywhere.
  • Demo video and slides: the video is a scripted recording of the real site (the same build that runs at aryasira.github.io/nasa), captioned and edited with Claude, and it carries a visible AI-assisted label. Claude also drafted the seven slides. The team reviewed both.
